items.summary: Version 2.0 is a substantive revision of version 1.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19174862). It supersedes the earlier procedural interpretation and its exclusion of competing explanations. The revised title is Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc. Reproduced descriptive findings are retained; failed model comparisons and photographic uncertainties are reported explicitly. The earlier version remains available through the record version history. We examine whether reproducible structural observations on the Phaistos Disc support a procedural interpretation. A pinned numerical transcription contains 242 main-sign positions, including one unreadable position, 45 readable sign types, 61 divider-defined groups and 18 supplementary stroke annotations. Source review reconciles counting and numbering conventions while retaining unresolved photographic uncertainty. The 02-to-12 side contrast persists after exact-family collapse. Adding side to a fixed position-only pairing predictor improves held-family loss by 0.082738 nats, but its exact conditional tail of 0.075 fails the frozen support rule. A positional mixture fails to outperform a bigram baseline. A separate directional test of the proposed 07-to-27 recovery relationship fails, with a one-sided permutation tail of 0.884. Supplementary-stroke comparisons have insufficient controlled overlap for the specified exact test. The work documents organization and constrains specific interpretations without establishing procedural functions or phonetic values. Corpus, code, protocols, full results and uncertainty ledgers accompany the paper.
items.title: Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc

items.summary: We develop a rigorous finite-dimensional mathematical framework connecting the renormalization group, gradient flows, Lyapunov stability, and noncooperative game theory. The central object is a renormalization-group flow written in gradient form, dg_i/dt = β_i(g) = - ∑_j G_ij(g) ∂Γ/∂g_j(g),          (1) where g = (g_1, …, g_n) belongs to an open domain M ⊂ ℝⁿ, Γ is a C² function, and G(g) is a symmetric positive-definite matrix. We associate to this flow a common-payoff game whose payoff is U(g) = - Γ(g).                   (2) We prove, with complete arguments, that ordinary Nash equilibria always imply renormalization-group fixed points, but the converse is false. We then identify the exact condition under which a fixed point becomes a genuine stable equilibrium of the game: a nondegenerate renormalization-group fixed point is asymptotically stable if and only if the Hessian of Γ is positive definite, if and only if it is a strict local minimum of Γ, if and only if it is a strict strong Nash equilibrium of U = -Γ. The distinction between ordinary Nash equilibrium and strong Nash equilibrium is essential. Ordinary Nash equilibria allow only unilateral deviations, while strong Nash equilibria exclude all small joint deviations. We provide explicit counterexamples showing that fixed points need not be Nash equilibria, that ordinary Nash equilibria need not be stable, and that invertibility of G alone does not imply finiteness of equilibria. We also prove global existence results under compactness and finiteness results under Morse nondegeneracy. The paper is self-contained at the level of multivariable calculus, linear algebra, ordinary differential equations, and basic Lyapunov stability theory. The framework is intentionally conditional: it does not claim that the gradient-flow representation has been proven in four-dimensional QCD or in any specific quantum field theory. Those issues are placed in a final section of open problems.
items.title: Gradient-Flow Renormalization Group as a Common-Potential Game: A Rigorous Equivalence Between Asymptotically Stable Fixed Points and Strict Strong Nash Equilibria

items.summary: This archive is provided as artifact material for the article "Synthesis and Verification of Register Automata over Data Sequences" for SETTA 2026. Abstract: Data sequences, such as time series, traces, and sensor streams, are words over large or infinite data domains. Their properties often depend on comparisons between values at different positions, which finite automata cannot express directly. We study synthesis and verification for Deterministic Register Automata (DRAs) over ordered data sequences. DRAs combine finite control with registers for remembered data values, providing compact symbolic descriptions of quantitative sequence languages. Our technical core is a local-search synthesis procedure and an exact robustness checker for DRAs. We fix the alphabet theory to ordered rationals $(\Q;<,=)$ with rational guard constants and use non-negative affine accumulator costs. For a fixed number of DRA registers, the checker runs in polynomial time; its dependence on that number is exponential. It reduces robustness to coverability and then to a shortest-path problem. Since the search ranges over $\Q^+$, it produces variable-length witnesses and, for RAA-definable alignment costs such as DTW, explores a counterexample space with no a priori length bound. As an application, we use learned DRAs as interpretable surrogates for queried neural sequence classifiers. A probably approximately correct (PAC) validation loop refines rejected candidates, returns genuine non-robustness witnesses for the classifier when found, and accepts a surrogate only with statistical guarantees for fidelity and local stability. We implement the framework in \textit{RAExc}, enabling the synthesis of interpretable automata and the verification of their robustness. We evaluate the approach on benchmark languages and sequentialized MNIST, demonstrating high accuracy while verifying the robustness of the learned automata.
items.title: Synthesis and Verification of Transformer Programs

A DOI evidence ledger distinguishes established component physics and published demonstrations from the original system-level hypotheses proposed here. items.summary: Automatic speaker verification (ASV) systems are highly vulnerable to presentation attacks, also called spoofing attacks. Replay is among the simplest attacks to mount - yet difficult to detect reliably. The generalization failure of spoofing countermeasures (CMs) has driven the community to study various alternative deep learning CMs. The majority of them are supervised approaches that learn a human-spoof discriminator. In this paper, we advocate a different, deep generative approach that leverages from powerful unsupervised manifold learning in classification. The potential benefits include the possibility to sample new data, and to obtain insights to the latent features of genuine and spoofed speech. To this end, we propose to use variational autoencoders (VAEs) as an alternative backend for replay attack detection, via three alternative models that differ in their class-conditioning. The first one, similar to the use of Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) in spoof detection, is to train independently two VAEs - one for each class. The second one is to train a single conditional model (C-VAE) by injecting a one-hot class label vector to the encoder and decoder networks. Our final proposal integrates an auxiliary classifier to guide the learning of the latent space. Our experimental results using constant-Q cepstral coefficient (CQCC) features on the ASVspoof 2017 and 2019 physical access subtask datasets indicate that the C-VAE offers substantial improvement in comparison to training two separate VAEs for each class. On the 2019 dataset, the C-VAE outperforms the VAE and the baseline GMM by an absolute 9 - 10% in both equal error rate (EER) and tandem detection cost function (t-DCF) metrics. Finally, we propose VAE residuals - the absolute difference of the original input and the reconstruction as features for spoofing detection.
items.title: Deep Generative Variational Autoencoding for Replay Spoof Detection in Automatic Speaker Verification

items.summary: Coding agents can now interpret a specification, implement it, write and execute tests, repair failures, and declare the result ready for release. When the same agentic system produces both the software and the evidence of its correctness, a passing test suite no longer constitutes independent evidence. Visible tests become an optimization target, and code, tests, and oracles may share a single misinterpretation of the specification. This paper argues that agent-produced software requires an assurance plane that is structurally independent of the build plane. We first characterize four gaps along the chain from stakeholder intent to production, namely the requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model gaps, and identify which of them verification can close. We then propose a framework that separates building from verifying, introduces a Verification Contract stating what must be demonstrated before release, and organizes verification in two phases: a specification-first phase designed without access to the implementation, and an implementation-aware phase that strengthens the evidence through mutation analysis, property-based testing, and fuzzing. The resulting evidence is consolidated into an assurance report that makes residual uncertainty explicit and leaves the release decision to a human. We evaluate the framework in a pre-registered study on three stateful services, two of them written by third-party models, and an EvalPlus pilot, comparing self-validation with independent verification under context-level and model-level independence. The builder's programs were correct, but its own tests missed subtle interactions: a verifier in a fresh context detected more of the 46 seeded faults than the builder's tests (Holm-corrected p = 0.006), and surfaced the ambiguities of the specification, at the price of rare false oracles. A verifier from another provider did not add detection. The framework and the study provide a basis for governing the release of software produced by agents.
items.title: Who Verifies the Builder? Toward Independent Assurance for Agent-Produced Software

items.summary: Audio deepfakes generated by neural text-to-speech and voice-cloning systems threaten speaker verification and public discourse at scale. The core challenge is cross-dataset generalization: detectors trained on one synthesis pipeline collapse on unseen forgeries. We argue that this failure is primarily because of structural synthetic speech artifacts which are multi-timescale trajectory anomalies. Though every existing detector aggregates a fixed-window frame statistics, this misaligns the architecture with the signal. We propose FlowFake, a Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) architecture whose hidden state evolves via a learned ODE, with per-neuron adaptive time constants simultaneously resolving spectral (10ms) and prosodic (2s) cues. At only 34K parameters FlowFake achieves formal BIBO stability and O(dt^4) integration error. On a four-dataset cross domain benchmark (ASVspoof2019-LA, FakeOrReal, InTheWild, MLAAD), FlowFake reaches 75.29% on ASVspoof2019 trained only on FakeOrReal and 79.97% trained only on MLAAD. It outperforms RawGAT-ST and Whisper-DF on every evaluated pair and matching SSL Wav2vec2 (300x larger) at 0.01% of its parameter count. The source code is available on : https://github.com/GhostRider2023/FlowFake
items.title: FlowFake: Liquid Networks for Audio Deepfake Detection

items.summary: We propose DeepASA, a multi-purpose model for auditory scene analysis that performs multi-input multi-output (MIMO) source separation, dereverberation, sound event detection (SED), audio classification, and direction-of-arrival estimation (DoAE) within a unified framework. DeepASA is designed for complex auditory scenes where multiple, often similar, sound sources overlap in time and move dynamically in space. To achieve robust and consistent inference across tasks, we introduce an object-oriented processing (OOP) strategy. This approach encapsulates diverse auditory features into object-centric representations and refines them through a chain-of-inference (CoI) mechanism. The pipeline comprises a dynamic temporal kernel-based feature extractor, a transformer-based aggregator, and an object separator that yields per-object features. These features feed into multiple task-specific decoders. Our object-centric representations naturally resolve the parameter association ambiguity inherent in traditional track-wise processing. However, early-stage object separation can lead to failure in downstream ASA tasks. To address this, we implement temporal coherence matching (TCM) within the chain-of-inference, enabling multi-task fusion and iterative refinement of object features using estimated auditory parameters. We evaluate DeepASA on representative spatial audio benchmark datasets, including ASA2, MC-FUSS, and STARSS23. Experimental results show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in both source separation and auditory parameter estimation under diverse spatial auditory scenes.
items.title: DeepASA: An Object-Oriented Multi-Purpose Network for Auditory Scene Analysis

items.summary: The Voynich Manuscript exhibits strong statistical regularities, but the distinction between recoverable grammar and recoverable lexical meaning remains unresolved. This study asks how far a progressively frozen, cross-validated analysis can reconstruct the manuscript’s internal word-building system without assigning meanings from illustrations, candidate languages, or post-hoc English paraphrase. Using canonical transcription, protected holdout partitions, alternate-transcription replication, exact host substitutions, and adversarial stopping rules, the analysis recovers a cumulative left-edge morphology, a transferable inventory of 39 surface CORE-0 stem/bodies, reproducible host-by-right-state coupling, a stable K/T referential contrast, and a directed network among powered lexical cores. The 39-core inventory predicts protected-frame combinatorics and content-blind contextual fingerprints out of sample, while attempts to decompose these bodies into a deeper transferable root layer fail. Nine recurring hosts show strongly replicated coupling to EY/EEY/EDY right-edge states, supporting a distributed morphological paradigm rather than independent left- and right-side systems. A 28-node directed CORE network also replicates across canonical calibration, untouched Holdout, and alternate-transcription tests, yielding neutral outbound- and inbound-biased stem classes without requiring part-of-speech or semantic assignments. On the project’s fully constrained 1,609-line benchmark, 12,299 of 12,495 positions are role-naturalizable (98.4314%), leaving 196 opaque positions. This percentage is explicitly a conditional benchmark-maturity statistic, not a measure of literal plaintext recovery or manuscript-wide translation accuracy. Repeated attempts to cross from structural organization to ordinary lexical meaning—including deeper-root induction, topic clustering, functional-neighborhood anchoring, local lexical syntax, illustration matching, source-language fitting, and prospective semantic transfer—fail the project’s promotion criteria. The resulting contribution is therefore a structural decipherment rather than a lexical one: a reproducible grammatical and morphological architecture together with an empirically identified lexical-identifiability ceiling. The work extends, but is distinct from, the earlier controlled-translation release at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22049207.
items.title: Structural Decipherment Without Lexical Recovery: A Cross-Validated Morphological Analysis of the Voynich Manuscript

items.summary: Image harmonization methods adjust the colour and lighting of an object pasted into a photograph so that it looks native to its new scene, and they are ranked by average error on one benchmark whose test images are real photographs with one object recoloured. One photograph can yield several such test images, and the benchmark promises that no photograph appears in both the training and the test split. We find that 1,399 photographs do, and the composites built on them are a quarter of the test set. Duplicate checks over file names or bytes miss this, because every composite is a different file. On that quarter the three methods we score end to end read two to five times lower error than on the rest, but most of the gap is composition rather than the sharing: the shared composites come almost entirely from one of the benchmark's four source collections, and inside that collection the gap falls to about one and a half times. An official score is therefore an average over two populations, mixed in a proportion the benchmark does not report. We release a test list of 5,581 composites whose construction identities do not appear in training, with four near-duplicate pairs disclosed rather than removed, adoptable without retraining at the price of one rescore per checkpoint. We leave open whether the sharing itself changes what a model learns. Contents of this record. The paper, the supplement, the LaTeX source of both, the record metadata and the licence statement. The identity matcher, the composite-locality and sensitivity checks, the CPU tests, the official iHarmony4 lists and the corrected test list are released under the MIT license at https://github.com/Buljic/only-means-only . What this record does not contain. No dataset, no images, no masks, no model checkpoints and no third-party baseline code or weights; those are described and cited by the paper and remain under their own terms. This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

items.summary: Singing Accompaniment Generation (SAG) is the process of generating instrumental music for a given clean vocal input. However, existing SAG techniques use source-separated vocals as input and overfit to separation artifacts. This creates a critical train-test mismatch, leading to failure on clean, real-world vocal inputs. We introduce AnyAccomp, a framework that resolves this by decoupling accompaniment generation from source-dependent artifacts. AnyAccomp first employs a quantized melodic bottleneck, using a chromagram and a VQ-VAE to extract a discrete and timbre-invariant representation of the core melody. A subsequent flow-matching model then generates the accompaniment conditioned on these robust codes. Experiments show AnyAccomp achieves competitive performance on separated-vocal benchmarks while significantly outperforming baselines on generalization test sets of clean studio vocals and, notably, solo instrumental tracks. This demonstrates a qualitative leap in generalization, enabling robust accompaniment for instruments - a task where existing models completely fail - and paving the way for more versatile music co-creation tools. Demo audio and code: https://anyaccomp.github.io
items.title: AnyAccomp: Generalizable Accompaniment Generation via Quantized Melodic Bottleneck

items.summary: This report establishes an exact conditional mathematical correspondence between a specified two-component phase model and the sine-Gordon equation appearing in a classical string-theory reduction. Developed within the Harmonic Physics Research Programme, the model uses interacting phase components labelled expansion and contraction in the proposed physical interpretation. For a continuum action with a cosine interaction, constant coefficients and equal component propagation speeds, an invertible change of variables separates the dynamics into an exact nonlinear sine-Gordon equation for the normalized relative phase and a free wave equation for the common phase. The interaction potential can also be expressed through the squared magnitude of the difference between two complex phase components. The derivation retains the full nonlinearity, extending the correspondence beyond the small-angle approximation. Direct numerical evolution of the original component fields provides a reproducible check at finite relative-phase amplitude. The reported breather benchmark reaches a peak relative-phase excursion of approximately 2.574 radians, with a maximum sampled error of approximately 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ radians over two oscillation periods. Component amplitudes remain fixed. Interaction-removal and unequal-speed controls document the failure to recover the same target when the specified conditions are changed. The string-theory connection is examined through the Pohlmeyer reduction of classical strings on R_t × S². A separate conventional kink embedding is checked against the local geometric constraints and string equations of motion. The evolved phase breather is not reconstructed as a string. The established result is a conditional correspondence between reduced classical equations; a full physical or quantum equivalence between the proposed phase model and string theory remains unestablished. Version 1.0 includes the standalone report and an accompanying reproducibility archive containing mathematical derivations, executable Python scripts, numerical settings, sampled synthetic data, control results, figures, source provenance, checksum manifests and reproduction instructions. A documented replay of the retained calculation and an AI-assisted computational audit support inspection and reuse of the reported results. items.summary: This archive is provided as artifact material for the article "Synthesis and Verification of Register Automata over Data Sequences" for SETTA 2026. Abstract: Data sequences, such as time series, traces, and sensor streams, are words over large or infinite data domains. Their properties often depend on comparisons between values at different positions, which finite automata cannot express directly. We study synthesis and verification for Deterministic Register Automata (DRAs) over ordered data sequences. DRAs combine finite control with registers for remembered data values, providing compact symbolic descriptions of quantitative sequence languages. Our technical core is a local-search synthesis procedure and an exact robustness checker for DRAs. We fix the alphabet theory to ordered rationals $(\Q;<,=)$ with rational guard constants and use non-negative affine accumulator costs. For a fixed number of DRA registers, the checker runs in polynomial time; its dependence on that number is exponential. It reduces robustness to coverability and then to a shortest-path problem. Since the search ranges over $\Q^+$, it produces variable-length witnesses and, for RAA-definable alignment costs such as DTW, explores a counterexample space with no a priori length bound. As an application, we use learned DRAs as interpretable surrogates for queried neural sequence classifiers. A probably approximately correct (PAC) validation loop refines rejected candidates, returns genuine non-robustness witnesses for the classifier when found, and accepts a surrogate only with statistical guarantees for fidelity and local stability. We implement the framework in \textit{RAExc}, enabling the synthesis of interpretable automata and the verification of their robustness. We evaluate the approach on benchmark languages and sequentialized MNIST, demonstrating high accuracy while verifying the robustness of the learned automata.
items.title: Synthesis and Verification of Transformer Programs

items.summary: Embedding enhancement improves speaker verification under acoustic mismatch without modifying a frozen backbone. Recent work has established a practical label-free setting for this task, but often adopts increasingly structured formulations. Here, the clean target is directly observed during training, making enhancement a matching problem on the unit hypersphere. We model the clean target with a von Mises--Fisher (vMF) likelihood and profile out a sample-wise concentration parameter, yielding a simple closed-form objective with adaptive weighting. Across VoxCeleb1, VoxSRC23, CN-Celeb, VOiCES, and VC-Mix, the proposed method largely preserves the baseline and gives clearer gains on challenging mismatch sets. It also remains stable under a broad single-view recipe, where a recent diffusion baseline becomes less reliable in controlled comparisons. These results suggest that effective label-free embedding enhancement in this setting does not require a highly structured formulation.
items.title: Revisiting Label-Free Speaker Embedding Enhancement with vMF Profile Likelihood

items.summary: Language-queried audio source separation (LASS) enables extracting any sound source using natural language. However, adapting LASS models to application-specific sound classes is challenging due to noisy training data and limited semantic coverage of the CLAP-based control signals. We propose a framework comprised of an automated data engine for training-data curation and a two-stage optimization process for class-specific CLAP control signals. Our objective evaluations across seven sound classes show that data refinement and control signal optimization consistently improve source separation performance. Subjective evaluation with 17 participants further demonstrates perceptual improvements of the model trained with optimized control signals over baseline and similar commercial models.
items.title: A Study on Improving Multi-class Audio Source Separation Via Decoupled CLAP Query Optimization and an Automated Data Engine

items.summary: Decentralized multi-robot shape formation in GPS-denied environments is important for search-and-rescue and disaster response. Conventional consensus-based formation controllers can violate safe separation, oscillate, or stall when communication degrades, sensors are noisy, or an agent drops out. This paper proposes a resilient decentralized controller that combines Huber-weighted consensus and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) state estimation with a Dual-Layer Artificial Potential Field (APF) safety barrier. The first layer adds an anti-symmetric lateral deflection to resolve head-on encounters between peers; the second applies a normal-plus-tangential circulation field around static obstacles. The framework is evaluated on five simulated nonholonomic differential-drive robots in Gazebo Harmonic (ROS 2 Jazzy). Three runs are compared: a linear consensus baseline, the same baseline under faults (15% packet loss, 50-150 ms delay, σ = 0.18 m sensor noise, and a mid-run agent blackout), and the proposed controller under the same faults. The fault-free baseline reached the pentagon fastest (0.0156 m final RMS error) but its minimum separation fell to 0.3918 m, with 31 logged violations of the 0.50 m margin. Under faults the baseline reached 0.0546 m with 5 violations (minimum 0.4833 m). The proposed controller recorded no violations, kept a minimum separation of 0.6757 m, and reached 0.0368 m final error, at the cost of slower convergence (about 21 s versus about 12-15 s). Results are from single simulation runs, and the safety barrier is empirical rather than formally guaranteed.
items.title: Resilient Decentralized Shape Formation of Multi-Robot Swarms Under Adversarial Real-World Faults in High-Complexity Disaster Environments

items.summary: Large language models often penalize multilingual users through hidden 'tokenizer taxes' caused by subword fragmentation. Geographic proper nouns offer a controlled stress case for this distributional asymmetry, as they are standardized, cross-linguistically available entities whose orthographic forms frequently mismatch tokenizer training distributions. We introduce the Cross-Linguistic Orthographic Uniqueness Score (CLOUS), a character-level metric based on Shannon surprisal that quantifies the orthographic rarity of localized country names. We evaluate CLOUS on a controlled corpus of 249 ISO-registered country names; generalization to other geographic entity types remains future work. We evaluate CLOUS against tokenization fertility for six production tokenizers spanning three algorithm families across eleven languages and seven script families. Using Spearman rank correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, CLOUS shows significant associative strength with fertility in 61 of 65 valid language-tokenizer combinations. As a screening tool for high-fragmentation entities, CLOUS achieves ROC-AUC = 0.850 and F1 = 0.740, correctly identifying approximately three-quarters of the highest-fragmentation entities from orthographic properties alone. We further show that CLOUS correlates with fertility more strongly than length-based baselines across all evaluated scripts, and outperforms a character bigram surprisal model in 69.2% of tested combinations, particularly for logographic, syllabic, and Latin scripts. Conversely, the bigram baseline proves superior for morphophonologically complex scripts like Arabic and Devanagari, indicating that tokenizer fragmentation is driven by local orthographic context in some scripts and absolute character rarity in others. Script family appears to be the primary driver of CLOUS-fertility correlation strength, with effect sizes ranging from modest for Latin-script languages ) to large for non-Latin scripts (   up to 0.686 for Japanese). These findings suggest that CLOUS may be useful as a lightweight pre-tokenization diagnostic for multilingual NLP pipelines.
items.title: Estimating Cross-Lingual Tokenization Fragmentation Risk: A Frequency-Based Uniqueness Score for Geographic Entities

items.summary: Version 2.0 is a substantive revision of version 1.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19174862). It supersedes the earlier procedural interpretation and its exclusion of competing explanations. The revised title is Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc. Reproduced descriptive findings are retained; failed model comparisons and photographic uncertainties are reported explicitly. The earlier version remains available through the record version history. We examine whether reproducible structural observations on the Phaistos Disc support a procedural interpretation. A pinned numerical transcription contains 242 main-sign positions, including one unreadable position, 45 readable sign types, 61 divider-defined groups and 18 supplementary stroke annotations. Source review reconciles counting and numbering conventions while retaining unresolved photographic uncertainty. The 02-to-12 side contrast persists after exact-family collapse. Adding side to a fixed position-only pairing predictor improves held-family loss by 0.082738 nats, but its exact conditional tail of 0.075 fails the frozen support rule. A positional mixture fails to outperform a bigram baseline. A separate directional test of the proposed 07-to-27 recovery relationship fails, with a one-sided permutation tail of 0.884. Supplementary-stroke comparisons have insufficient controlled overlap for the specified exact test. The work documents organization and constrains specific interpretations without establishing procedural functions or phonetic values. Corpus, code, protocols, full results and uncertainty ledgers accompany the paper.
items.title: Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc

items.summary: The following dataset contains images and band count estimates of shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) vertebrae. It is intended to assist with the replication of the results for the study: Automated reading of vertebral images for aging shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) using Bayesian deep learning. Samples were obtained from two primary sources: recreational game fishing competitions primarily from the North Island between 1994 and 2003, and through the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) Fisheries Observer Programme between 2002 and 2003, primarily from the South Island (Bishop et al., 2006). Shortfin mako vertebrae images (n=146, belonging to 131 unique sharks) were obtained from previous ageing studies using band counts (Bishop et al., 2006; Francis, 2016). Most vertebrae images were of half bow-tie section pairs. These section pairs were filtered by image quality with lower quality images being excluded, resulting in a reduced dataset of 133 section pairs. Each section pair was isolated, resulting in a complete dataset of 266 half bow-tie section images. We compared the following three deep learning methods: DeepEnsembling, a mixture of Laplace approximations, and multi-stochastic weight average Gaussian to predict the band counts by human readers using a dataset of 146 images of shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) vertebrae. Multi-stochastic weight average Gaussian offered marginally superior predictive power and uncertainty calibration, and its predictions typically matched estimates provided by human readers. We conclude that the application of deep learning for automated vertebrae reading demonstrated strong initial promise.

items.summary: LONGITUDINAL DEVICE MIGRATION AND MEANING CONTINUITY AT THE LIMIT Device Replacement × Model Bridging × Control Semantics STARLI RESEARCH WORKS | INSTITUTE XXIV | FLAGSHIP 24 Feng Cheng-en 33 × Starli Research Works This research monograph investigates a deceptively difficult question in long-term brain–computer interfaces: when sensors, acquisition electronics, firmware, electrode geometry, or decoding models change, what would justify the claim that a user's task-grounded control meaning has been preserved? Numerical signal alignment alone cannot establish continuity of intention. Two systems may encode different signals while supporting the same functional command, or produce nearly identical latent representations while mapping to incompatible actions. The volume formulates meaning continuity as a conditional, falsifiable engineering and scientific hypothesis. It connects device-specific observation models, neural recording instability, task and action ontologies, paired old/new sensing periods, latent manifold bridging, longitudinal recalibration, calibrated abstention, functional validation, and an accessible right to reject the proposed migration. Its central commitment is that no amount of predictive accuracy can compensate for invalid authorization, an unverified physical reference, or loss of independent control. The research atlas comprises thirty connected mathematical derivations, eighty-two research chapters, and 410 independently paginated chapter sections that examine observables, inverse explanations, discriminating experiments, uncertainty and noncompensable safeguards, and independent requalification. Two hundred detailed Research Gates propose future falsification and handoff programs, while thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos preserve revisable candidate approaches rather than immutable conclusions. A claim-scoped DOI evidence ledger connects the study to published work on neural recording drift, decoder adaptation, manifold alignment, longitudinal neural interfaces, speech BCIs, user preferences, and neurotechnology ethics. items.summary: Metascience uses a scientific approach to understand and improve science. Critical metascience takes a step back to question metascience’s common assumptions, methods, problems, and solutions. In this article, I aim to raise the profile of critical metascience and offer a rationale for viewing it as a distinct area of multidisciplinary inquiry. I define critical metascience, explain why it is important, and address some potential concerns about it. I also consider some emerging themes in the area and evaluate its potential relationships with metascience. I conclude that there needs to be greater recognition of critical metascience and greater interaction between metascience and critical metascience in order to improve metascience’s objectivity and approach.
items.title: What is critical metascience and why is it important?

items.summary: Popper’s (1983, 2002) philosophy of science has enjoyed something of a renaissance in the wake of the replication crisis, offering a philosophical basis for the ensuing science reform movement. However, adherence to Popper’s approach may also be at least partly responsible for the sense of “crisis” that has developed following multiple unexpected replication failures. In this article, I contrast Popper’s approach with that of Lakatos (1978) as well as with a related but problematic approach called naïve methodological falsificationism (NMF; Lakatos, 1978). The Popperian approach is powerful because it is based on logical refutations, but its theories are noncausal and, therefore, potentially lacking in scientific value. In contrast, the Lakatosian approach considers causal theories, but it concedes that these theories are not logically refutable. Finally, NMF represents a hybrid approach that subjects Lakatosian causal theories to Popperian logical refutations. However, its tactic of temporarily accepting a ceteris paribus clause during theory testing may be viewed as scientifically inappropriate, epistemically inconsistent, and “completely redundant” (Lakatos, 1978, p. 40). I conclude that the replication “crisis” makes the most sense in the context of the Popperian and NMF approaches because it is only in these two approaches that the failure to replicate a previously corroborated theory represents a logical refutation of that theory. In contrast, such replication failures are less problematic in the Lakatosian approach because they do not logically refute theories. Indeed, in the Lakatosian approach, replication failures can be temporarily ignored or used to motivate theory development.
items.title: The replication crisis is less of a "crisis" in Lakatos' philosophy of science than it is in Popper's.

items.summary: This paper offers a candidate descriptive model based on the author’s retrospective account of internal agent-like experience during a past period of social isolation, emotional distress and perceived high cognitive load. The Opposition–Load–Coupling vocabulary organizes reported phases of self-talk, opposition, felt load, perceived coupling, autonomy, boundary degradation and disengagement. These are reported experiences and interpretive constructs, not demonstrated causal mechanisms. Claimed benefits and harms are unmeasured first-person reports. The Shared Value Anchor is an untested candidate predictor, not an established stabilizer or necessary condition. The case does not establish whether value conflict preceded initial boundary degradation or distinguish the proposal from a simpler load-based account. The model is situated alongside dialogical-self, Internal Family Systems, predictive-processing, imaginary-companion, writer-agency and tulpa literature. Any incremental contribution lies in the proposed coupling vocabulary and separately testable value-anchor hypothesis, not in discovering internal multiplicity or proving a new mechanism. Safety: do not intentionally induce or replicate the conditions described. This is the author’s own past experience, published at the author’s direction; no formal ethics approval or exemption is claimed. Version 4 incorporates author-adopted revisions following advisory and changed-text checks, including prior-involved AI reviewers. Those checks are not independent peer review, clinical validation or evidence of effectiveness.

items.summary: Audio deepfakes generated by neural text-to-speech and voice-cloning systems threaten speaker verification and public discourse at scale. The core challenge is cross-dataset generalization: detectors trained on one synthesis pipeline collapse on unseen forgeries. We argue that this failure is primarily because of structural synthetic speech artifacts which are multi-timescale trajectory anomalies. Though every existing detector aggregates a fixed-window frame statistics, this misaligns the architecture with the signal. We propose FlowFake, a Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) architecture whose hidden state evolves via a learned ODE, with per-neuron adaptive time constants simultaneously resolving spectral (10ms) and prosodic (2s) cues. At only 34K parameters FlowFake achieves formal BIBO stability and O(dt^4) integration error. On a four-dataset cross domain benchmark (ASVspoof2019-LA, FakeOrReal, InTheWild, MLAAD), FlowFake reaches 75.29% on ASVspoof2019 trained only on FakeOrReal and 79.97% trained only on MLAAD. It outperforms RawGAT-ST and Whisper-DF on every evaluated pair and matching SSL Wav2vec2 (300x larger) at 0.01% of its parameter count. The source code is available on : https://github.com/GhostRider2023/FlowFake
items.title: FlowFake: Liquid Networks for Audio Deepfake Detection

items.summary: We propose DeepASA, a multi-purpose model for auditory scene analysis that performs multi-input multi-output (MIMO) source separation, dereverberation, sound event detection (SED), audio classification, and direction-of-arrival estimation (DoAE) within a unified framework. DeepASA is designed for complex auditory scenes where multiple, often similar, sound sources overlap in time and move dynamically in space. To achieve robust and consistent inference across tasks, we introduce an object-oriented processing (OOP) strategy. This approach encapsulates diverse auditory features into object-centric representations and refines them through a chain-of-inference (CoI) mechanism. The pipeline comprises a dynamic temporal kernel-based feature extractor, a transformer-based aggregator, and an object separator that yields per-object features. These features feed into multiple task-specific decoders. Our object-centric representations naturally resolve the parameter association ambiguity inherent in traditional track-wise processing. However, early-stage object separation can lead to failure in downstream ASA tasks. To address this, we implement temporal coherence matching (TCM) within the chain-of-inference, enabling multi-task fusion and iterative refinement of object features using estimated auditory parameters. We evaluate DeepASA on representative spatial audio benchmark datasets, including ASA2, MC-FUSS, and STARSS23. Experimental results show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in both source separation and auditory parameter estimation under diverse spatial auditory scenes.
items.title: DeepASA: An Object-Oriented Multi-Purpose Network for Auditory Scene Analysis

items.summary: This repository provides the datasets, pretrained models and generated network parameters used in the manuscript “DiffPINN: Generative diffusion-initialized physics-informed neural networks for accelerating seismic wavefield representation.” The accompanying source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/DeepWave-KAUST/DiffPINN-pub DiffPINN is a latent diffusion framework that generates initialization parameters for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) used in frequency-domain seismic wavefield modeling. A set of PINNs is first trained across diverse velocity models and their parameters are flattened into one-dimensional vectors. An autoencoder compresses the length of these vectors into multi-channel latent tensors, and a conditional diffusion model is trained on those tensors with the velocity model and source configuration as conditions. At inference, the diffusion model generates a latent tensor for a new velocity model, with a physics-based gradient correction applied at each reverse step, and the decoder turns it into a complete set of PINN parameters. The archived files are organized as follows. dataset.zip After extraction, dataset.zip contains five folders corresponding to the five stages of the framework: metatrain/ : contains meta_train.mat , the dataset used for meta-training. pinntrain/ : contains pinntrain1.mat to pinntrain2600.mat , one file per velocity model, used to train the 2600 PINNs that form the parameter dataset. aetrain/ : contains the flattened parameters of the 2600 converged PINNs, used to train the autoencoder. difftrain/ : contains the latent tensors encoded from those parameters, used to train the diffusion model. pinntest/ : contains CurveVelA.mat , Layer.mat and FlatFaultA.mat , the three test velocity models used to reproduce the results reported in the manuscript. All data are stored in MATLAB .mat format. Each .mat file contains the following variables: x_train , z_train , sx_train : the spatial coordinates and source locations of the collocation samples. m_train , m0_train : the squared slowness of the medium and of the homogeneous background. u0_real_train , u0_imag_train : the real and imaginary parts of the analytical background wavefield. x_test , z_test , sx_test : the coordinates of the full evaluation grid. du_real_test , du_imag_test : the real and imaginary parts of the numerical reference solution. The training velocity models are drawn from the CurveVel-A class of the OpenFWI benchmark dataset, resized to 101×101 with a grid spacing of 25 m and mildly smoothed. All wavefields are computed at 5 Hz. The reference solutions are obtained with the optimized nine-point frequency-domain finite-difference scheme of Jo et al. (1996). Among the three test models, CurveVelA is drawn from the training distribution, while Layer (a layered section of the Marmousi model) and FlatFaultA lie outside it. Because aetrain/ and difftrain/ are the outputs of the two preceding stages, users can start at any point in the pipeline rather than rebuilding the parameter dataset, which takes roughly 65 hours on ten V100 GPUs. trained_model.zip After extraction, trained_model.zip contains the three trained models used to reproduce the results in the manuscript: meta_trained.pth : the meta-learned PINN initialization, trained for 40000 iterations over 500 velocity models. ae_trained.pth : the autoencoder, trained for 1000 epochs on the 2600 flattened parameter vectors. diff_trained.pt : the conditional diffusion model, trained for 400000 iterations on the latent tensors. generated_weight.zip After extraction, generated_weight.zip contains the latent tensors generated by the trained diffusion model for the three test velocity models: CurveVelA_weight.mat : generated parameters for the in-distribution CurveVel-A model. Layer_weight.mat : generated parameters for the layered Marmousi model. FlatFaultA_weight.mat : generated parameters for the FlatFault-A model. These were produced

items.summary: Speaker verification (SV) performance degrades under language mismatch due to the entanglement of speaker identity with language-specific acoustic cues. To address this problem, we leverage large-scale self-supervised pre-trained models (PTMs) to learn language-agnostic speaker representations. We utilize PTMs as robust front-end feature extractors, capitalizing on their rich acoustic and linguistic knowledge acquired from vast, diverse audio data. These generalized features are then used to train a downstream speaker embedding network, effectively disentangling speaker identity from language-specific characteristics. We validate our approach on the TidyVoice2026 benchmark, which benchmarks SV under language mismatch. Our proposed system (team T02) achieves equal error rates (EERs) of 2.21% on tv26_eval-A and 2.99% on tv26_eval-U.
items.title: Cross-Lingual Speaker Verification with Self-Supervised Pre-Trained Models

items.summary: The goal of single-channel source separation is to reconstruct $K$ sources given their mixture. In supervised settings where vast amounts of clean source data are available, this challenging, ill-posed problem has been addressed successfully by generative diffusion and flow-based prior models. However, access to such clean source samples is often limited, and even when available, supervised models are vulnerable to domain shifts. To bridge this gap, we present Separation via Unsupervised Remixing Flow (SURF), an unsupervised flow matching approach for source separation that learns directly from observed mixtures. This method relies on a novel combination of state-of-the-art supervised flow matching and regression-based self-supervised techniques. At a high level, starting from a teacher model, we utilize a "remixing" step to bootstrap the learning of a student flow model from the teacher's estimates. We provide insights into the objectives optimized by this approach and draw a novel connection to the Wake-Sleep algorithm. Empirical evaluations on image and audio benchmarks demonstrate that SURF establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming existing unsupervised methods. See our demo page for examples. https://google.github.io/df-conformer/surf/
items.title: SURF: Separation via Unsupervised Remixing Flow

items.summary: Loss and phase jitter told apart from squeezing pairs at several pump levels, resonances split by backscattering, a wrong error bar of the transmission fit fixed, a faster photonic-molecule model, two test tolerances tied to their floating-point limits, and a third tutorial. Fixed fit_resonance_transmission(..., branch=...) gave wrong error bars for kappa_ex_hz and kappa_0_hz . The derivative of the escape efficiency with respect to the dip depth D, which is -1 / (4 sqrt(1 - D)) on the over-coupled branch and +1 / (4 sqrt(1 - D)) on the under-coupled one, had the opposite sign on both, which flipped the term that carries the (strong, negative) correlation of the linewidth and the depth. Over-coupled ring ( kappa = 100 MHz , eta = 0.8 , 121 points over +/- 300 MHz, 1 % noise): kappa_0_hz_sigma 0.325 MHz -> 0.171 MHz (Monte Carlo scatter of 400 scans: 0.166 MHz), kappa_ex_hz_sigma 0.768 MHz -> 0.946 MHz (scatter 0.900 MHz). Under-coupled ring ( eta = 0.3 ): kappa_ex_hz_sigma 0.427 MHz -> 0.197 MHz (scatter 0.189 MHz), kappa_0_hz_sigma 0.452 MHz -> 0.735 MHz (scatter 0.695 MHz). The fitted values, kappa_hz , eta_esc and eta_sigma were right and are unchanged. Test: test_kappa_ex_and_kappa_0_error_bars . Added fit_squeezing_pairs(sq_db, anti_db, sigma_db, sigma_anti_db=None, fit_jitter=True, dark_noise=0, dark_in_reference=False) : the total efficiency and the local-oscillator phase jitter shared by squeezed / antisqueezed pairs measured at several pump levels, with error bars, each pair's source level, and a chi-square check. One pair cannot separate loss from jitter ( infer_source needs the jitter given); several pairs can, because loss pulls every pair toward shot noise by the same fraction while jitter mixes in a part of the antisqueezing, which grows with the pump. Model: a pure source per pair (no law between pump power and gain assumed), the jitter law of phase_noise_variance , then the efficiency and a stated dark noise as in detected_variance . Checked against the package's own forward path (the output of single_mode_parametric behind an escape efficiency, at three analysis frequencies, is exactly such a source: efficiency to 1e-8, jitter to a relative 1e-6), against infer_source for one pair without jitter (relative 1e-10), and by 150 seeded noisy sets (scatter 0.75 to 1.3 times the error bars). The analysis follows how experiments describe loss and jitter, for example B. Shajilal et al., arXiv:2211.06632 (2022), who model their squeezing and antisqueezing against pump power with a total efficiency and a jitter angle. README example 24. split_transmission(...) and fit_split_resonance(f_hz, transmission, sigma, fit_slope=False) : a through-port dip split into a doublet by backscattering, the coupled-mode model of the clockwise and counterclockwise modes of T. J. Kippenberg, S. M. Spillane and K. J. Vahala, Opt. Lett. 27, 1669 (2002). Returns the linewidth of each standing-wave mode, the escape efficiency, the splitting and the center with error bars, for the under- and the over-coupled regime (a resolved doublet is not symmetric under eta -> 1 - eta , so a regime that does not fit is reported as such), and their chi-square difference. The transmission is derived in the sqzcomb.resonance docstring and checked against the drift matrix of photonic_molecule (relative 1e-13 at 140 points), noise-free recovery (1e-8) and 40 seeded noisy scans. fit_resonance_transmission now names it when it refuses a doublet.
